The foundations chapter derived [Bayes' rule](../foundations/bayes-rule.qmd), and the frequentist sequence distinguished a [likelihood from a probability distribution over observations](maximum-likelihood.qmd#probability-and-likelihood). We now combine the two to construct a posterior distribution from an observed linguistic resource.

First, keep the random and observed objects separate. $\mathbf Z$ denotes the binary random sample and $\mathbf z$ the values we observed. $\Theta$ denotes the unknown superpopulation parameter. Before seeing $\mathbf z$, the prior density distributes model-based uncertainty over $\Theta$; after seeing $\mathbf z$, the posterior density redistributes that uncertainty using the likelihood.

The conditioning bar uses the [conditional-probability](../foundations/conditional-probability.qmd) operation: the reference distribution for $\Theta$ changes after restricting attention to the observed data. The Bernoulli likelihood below also assumes [conditional independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) of the cell indicators given their shared probability.

We will work through the update in detail. After specifying a Bernoulli superpopulation model, we will multiply its likelihood by a beta prior and calculate the normalizing constant. Then we will ask which statements concern $\Theta$, which concern the finite Turkish resource, and which depend on whether the sampling model is adequate.

## A Bernoulli superpopulation model

We use the [Turkish UniMorph table](https://github.com/unimorph/tur). Pimentel et al. ([2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.sigmorphon-1.25/)) describe its use in a morphological reinflection task, and Batsuren et al. ([2022](https://aclanthology.org/2022.lrec-1.89/)) describe UniMorph as a type-level resource of lemma--form--feature triples.

The prepared table retains 588 distinct verb lexemes with one form in the feature cell `V;IND;PST;3;SG;POS;DECL`. Each row represents one lexeme--paradigm cell and contains no usage count. The binary variable $Z_i$ marks whether the final two orthographic characters extracted during preparation begin with *t*. Because the extraction does not consult a morphological segmentation, it measures a word-form ending. A morpheme-boundary claim would require an annotation the table does not supply.

```{r}
#| label: load-unimorph-posterior
library(ggplot2)

population <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-population.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
sample_120 <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-sample-120.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

N <- nrow(population)
K <- sum(population$t_initial)
n <- nrow(sample_120)
k <- sum(sample_120$t_initial)
resource_share <- K / N

stopifnot(
  N == 588L, K == 200L, n == 120L, k == 42L,
  !anyDuplicated(population$lemma),
  all(sample_120$lemma %in% population$lemma)
)

data.frame(N, K, n, k, resource_share, sample_share = k / n)
```

The value $K/N=$ `r sprintf("%.6f", resource_share)` is known because all 588 rows in the analyzed UniMorph table are available. There is no posterior uncertainty about that finite-population proportion.

### Exchangeability and IID sampling {#exchangeability-and-iid}

A sequence is **exchangeable** when reordering its entries does not change
their joint probability. Under that assumption, row order carries no model
information: a sequence with 42 focal endings receives the same probability
as any reordering with the same 42 focal endings. Exchangeability can still
allow dependence among the entries.

**Independent and identically distributed (IID)** sampling is stronger.
*Identically distributed* says that every $Z_i$ has the same Bernoulli
probability $\theta$; *independent* says that learning one $Z_i$ does not
change the conditional distribution of another after $\theta$ is fixed. IID
sampling implies exchangeability, while exchangeability alone does not imply
IID sampling. The model below makes the stronger IID assumption conditional
on the shared parameter $\Theta$.

To introduce Bayesian updating, we posit an exchangeable superpopulation from which lexeme cells are independently drawn,

$$
Z_i\mid\Theta=\theta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta),
\qquad
\Theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1).
$$

The 120 observed rows were drawn without replacement from the known 588-row
table. The exchangeable Bernoulli model instead imagines independent draws from
an unlimited population with a shared unknown probability. Its posterior thus
answers a counterfactual superpopulation question rather than reconstructing the
without-replacement procedure that selected the observed rows.

The $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ density equals one on $0<\theta<1$. It is support-compatible and convenient, but it is not uniquely “uninformative”: a prior uniform in $\theta$ is not uniform after a nonlinear transformation such as the log odds. We use it here to make the updating calculation transparent.

## Updating a continuous parameter

Bayes' rule for a continuous parameter is

$$
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
=
\frac{
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)f_\Theta(\theta)
}{
p_{\mathbf Z}(\mathbf z)
}.
$$

The denominator

$$
p_{\mathbf Z}(\mathbf z)
=
\int_0^1
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
f_\Theta(\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta
$$

normalizes the numerator. For $k$ focal cells among $n$ exchangeable Bernoulli observations, conditional independence gives the full likelihood

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
&=
\prod_{i=1}^n
\theta^{z_i}(1-\theta)^{1-z_i}\\
&=
\theta^{\sum_i z_i}(1-\theta)^{n-\sum_i z_i}\\
&=
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the probability of the observed binary sequence. If we modeled only the unordered count $K=k$, a binomial coefficient would also appear; because that coefficient does not depend on $\theta$, both representations produce the same posterior shape.

The normalized $\operatorname{Beta}(a,b)$ prior is

$$
f_\Theta(\theta)
=
\frac{1}{B(a,b)}
\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1},
\qquad 0<\theta<1.
$$

Substituting the likelihood and prior into continuous Bayes' rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
&=
\frac{
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}
\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}/B(a,b)
}{
\int_0^1
u^k(1-u)^{n-k}
u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}/B(a,b)
\,\mathrm du
}\\[4pt]
&=
\frac{
\theta^{a+k-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-k-1}
}{B(a+k,b+n-k)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality uses the definition of the beta function in the denominator. Thus, without dropping the normalizing constant,

$$
\Theta\mid\mathbf Z=\mathbf z
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(a+k,b+n-k).
$$

The shorter kernel calculation is

$$
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
\propto
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.
$$

Multiplying by the $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ prior gives

$$
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
\propto
\theta^{1+k-1}(1-\theta)^{1+n-k-1},
$$

so the exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model posterior is

$$
\Theta\mid\mathbf z
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(1+k,1+n-k).
$$

The equation-to-code bridge is literal: `posterior_alpha <- prior_alpha + k` computes $a+k$, `posterior_beta <- prior_beta + n - k` computes $b+n-k$, and `dbeta(theta_grid, posterior_alpha, posterior_beta)` evaluates the normalized density on the grid.

```{r}
#| label: compute-unimorph-posterior
prior_alpha <- 1
prior_beta <- 1
posterior_alpha <- prior_alpha + k
posterior_beta <- prior_beta + n - k

theta_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1001L)
posterior_density <- data.frame(
  theta = theta_grid,
  prior = dbeta(theta_grid, prior_alpha, prior_beta),
  posterior = dbeta(theta_grid, posterior_alpha, posterior_beta)
)

stopifnot(posterior_alpha == 43L, posterior_beta == 79L)
data.frame(posterior_alpha, posterior_beta)
```

The 42 observed *t*-initial cells and 78 other cells update the prior to a beta distribution with shape parameters `r posterior_alpha` and `r posterior_beta`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-unimorph-posterior
#| fig-cap: "Prior and exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation posterior densities. The vertical line marks the known proportion in the complete 588-row UniMorph table."
posterior_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(theta = theta_grid, density = posterior_density$prior,
             distribution = "prior"),
  data.frame(theta = theta_grid, density = posterior_density$posterior,
             distribution = "posterior")
)

ggplot(posterior_long, aes(theta, density, linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = resource_share, color = "grey35", linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Modeled share of lexeme cells with a t-initial ending",
       y = "Density", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

For a continuous parameter, the density at one point is not a point probability. Posterior probabilities are integrals over intervals:

$$
\mathbb{P}(a<\Theta<b\mid\mathbf z)
=
\int_a^b
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)\,\mathrm d\theta.
$$

The shorter statement $f(\theta\mid\mathbf z)\propto p(\mathbf z\mid\theta)f(\theta)$ identifies posterior shape, but a normalized density is required before we assign such probabilities.

## What the posterior does not say

The likelihood evaluates the fixed sample as a function of $\theta$; the posterior distributes model-based uncertainty over $\theta$ after conditioning on that sample. Neither quantity changes the known resource proportion. UniMorph supplies types, not token frequencies, so this posterior does not estimate the frequency of *t*-initial past endings in Turkish use.

## Recap and forward link

1. The likelihood holds the observed sample $\mathbf z$ fixed and varies as a function of candidate $\theta$ values.
2. The posterior is the normalized product of likelihood and prior.
3. Conditional independence reduces the Bernoulli sequence likelihood to powers determined by $k$ and $n-k$.
4. The $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ prior is convenient and transparent, but not uniquely noninformative.

The [posterior-summaries page](posterior-summaries.qmd#credible-intervals-and-directional-probabilities) asks which distinct claims can be extracted from this posterior.

## Check your understanding

1. Which quantity is fixed when the likelihood is evaluated?
2. Why is $200/588$ not uncertain in this analysis?
3. Which assumption makes the exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model a counterfactual model rather than a description of the observed sample?
4. Why is a posterior density at one value not a point probability?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The observed sample $\mathbf z$, including $n=120$ and $k=42$, is fixed while the likelihood varies over $\theta$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The complete UniMorph table is observed, so its 200 focal rows and 588 total rows are fixed counts rather than uncertain parameters. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model assumes independent, exchangeable Bernoulli draws from a superpopulation, while the observed sample was drawn without replacement from the known 588-row table. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. For a continuous parameter, probability is an integral over an interval; a density value at one point is not probability mass at that point. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
